analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workers' rights to form unions and bargain collectively, with tougher penalties on employers who violate labor law.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 219 cosponsors in the House, including 3 Republicans, but was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it easier for workers to unionize and bargain. It would reclassify many independent contractors and gig workers as employees, allow fines up to $50,000 per violation against employers who fire or retaliate against union supporters, let unions collect fees from all workers in a unit even in states that ban it, and let newly certified unions get binding arbitration for a first contract if bargaining stalls. It also would let workers vote in union elections by phone or internet and ban forced anti-union meetings.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to organize: the bill reclassifies many contractors as covered employees [S2][S3], lets union organizers collect fees from everyone in a bargaining unit even where state law forbids it [S2][S3], bans employer meetings designed to discourage union membership [S2][S3], bars companies from requiring workers to waive class-action rights [S2][S3], protects strikers from permanent replacement [S2][S3], and adds whistleblower protections and remote electronic voting in union elections [S2][S3]. It also gives workers real money damages — back pay without reduction, doubled liquidated damages, and civil fines against violators — where current law offers little more than reinstatement [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Reclassifies many independent contractors as employees covered by labor protections, using a test requiring the worker to be free from control, outside the employer's usual business, and independently established

Imposes civil penalties up to $50,000 per unfair labor practice — doubled to $100,000 for repeat violators — and lets fired workers sue for back pay, consequential damages, and doubled liquidated damages, where current law generally provides only reinstatement and back pay
Bans employers from requiring or coercing workers to attend meetings designed to discourage union membership, and voids agreements that force employees to give up class-action rights
Protects strikers from permanent replacement and discrimination, allows secondary strikes, and permits union fee agreements that override state right-to-work laws
Requires binding arbitration for a first union contract if bargaining stalls after 90 days plus mediation, and lets workers vote in representation elections by phone or internet
Adds whistleblower protections for employees, including managers, who report labor-law violations, with reinstatement, back pay, and compensatory damages

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially large companies, gig-economy platforms, staffing firms, and franchised businesses — would face higher labor costs, union organizing they currently can resist through mandatory meetings and litigation-waiver agreements, fines for violations, and possible arbitration of first contracts. Business groups have long opposed this bill on those grounds.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face materially higher costs and less control over their workforce: fines up to $50,000 per violation, binding arbitration of first contracts, joint-employer exposure for franchise and staffing arrangements, and restrictions on replacing strikers

The bill would override state right-to-work laws by letting contracts force all employees in a unit to pay union fees, which supporters of those laws view as compelling workers to fund organizations they chose not to join

Reclassifying contractors as employees would remove the independent status of some gig and freelance workers, including flexibility over hours and clients, a cost honest supporters of the bill acknowledge

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want to organize, the gains are substantial: real penalties, damages, faster elections, and protections that current law lacks, in a system where violations are now largely consequence-free. The costs fall on employers, who would pay more and lose some control, and a share of that cost could show up in prices or hiring. The right-to-work override is the most contested feature: it forces objecting workers to pay fees in states that banned that practice. The independent-contractor reclassification trades flexibility for coverage. On balance, the bill shifts bargaining power clearly toward workers and unions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the same day, and the committee — controlled by the new Republican majority — never took it up, so it died there when Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 20 was introduced on February 28, 2023 by Rep. Bobby Scott with 219 cosponsors, including 216 Democrats and 3 Republicans
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce
The complete action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no Senate companion action listed for this bill
An essentially identical bill, H.R. 842 in the 117th Congress, passed the House in March 2021 when Democrats held the majority but was never taken up by the Senate

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced higher labor costs, fines, and easier union organizing are better off because the bill never advanced. House Republican leadership and the committee chair, who never scheduled action, achieved the outcome they sought without ever having to vote on the record.

for.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-VA), lead sponsor and ranking member of the Education and Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 20 on February 28, 2023 and recruited 218 original cosponsors

for.name: 216 House Democrats and 3 Republicans (including Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill majority support in the House on paper

for.name: AFL-CIO and organized labor
for.what_they_did: Publicly championed the PRO Act, named for former AFL-CIO president Richard Trumka, and pressed Congress to pass it

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce Republican majority
against.role: Committee of referral, holding the gavel
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on H.R. 20 during the entire Congress, leaving it in committee until the session ended

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the floor calendar and never brought the bill up, consistent with the committee's inaction

against.name: Business and employer coalitions (U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied trade groups)
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the PRO Act, arguing it would raise labor costs, undermine right-to-work laws, and reclassify independent contractors

sides.party_line_note: The 219 cosponsors split 216 Democrats to 3 Republicans; the committee that buried it was run by the Republican majority, and no votes on the bill were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would impose fines up to $50,000 per violation, ban mandatory anti-union meetings, and let workers sue for doubled damages, directly raising the cost of opposing union drives. Companies that currently face little penalty for firing organizers would lose that advantage.

The strict employee test would pull many gig and contract workers under union and labor-law coverage, ending their classification as independent contractors. These businesses' models depend on contractor status.

industries.industry: Franchisors and joint-employer-dependent industries (fast food, hotels)
industries.note: A broad joint-employer definition covering indirect and reserved control would make parent companies bargains with unions over franchisee workers. This expands their exposure to labor liability.

Unions would get fee agreements enforceable over state right-to-work laws, secondary strikes, binding arbitration for first contracts, and electronic voting that speeds elections. Union membership and finances would grow if the bill passed.
Reclassification would give some contractors union and labor-law protections but take away independent status, including control over their own schedules and clients.
